title: Speed–Accuracy Trade-Off
summary: Perform an untimed discrimination task, then compare four fictional respondents. A caution slider moves speed and accuracy together while ability is held constant.
learningObjectives: Explain why a single outcome measure cannot separate ability from response caution.
Read a joint speed-accuracy plot and locate a respondent on the trade-off curve.
Distinguish a drift-rate (ability) difference from a threshold (strategy) difference.
Explain why reaction-time distributions make the mean and median disagree.
Recognise exclusion cut-offs and correct-trials-only decisions as researcher choices that can move a result.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trials are scored in the browser tab only, nothing is retained after a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: No trial is ever timed out: the stimulus persists until answered, nothing flashes, and the key mapping is stated before any block begins. Untimed practice with feedback runs first. Responses use the Left and Right arrow keys or two large buttons of at least 3.5rem height, so the task is fully operable by keyboard, pointer or touch. The arrow display is aria-hidden and paired with a sentence giving the counts, so a trial is answerable without perceiving nine small glyphs. A complete non-timed route exists: the fictional-strategy simulator and the caution slider reach every conclusion on the page without performing the task, and the page says so before it starts. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a table stating drift rate and threshold outright; the respondent who differs in ability is drawn hollow as well as differently coloured. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Speed-accuracy trade-off: why one outcome measure cannot separate ability from response caution
simulationNotes: Fictional respondents use the standard closed form for an unbiased diffusion process: expected accuracy is the logistic of 2*drift*threshold, and expected decision time is (threshold/drift)*tanh(drift*threshold) plus a non-decision constant. Three respondents share a drift rate and differ only in threshold, so their differing scores are purely strategic; a fourth differs in drift rate instead. No participant, dataset or published parameter estimate is represented. The student's own block is 16 trials, far too few for any real estimate, on browser timing that carries tens of milliseconds of noise. The tool measures nothing about the user: not intelligence, impulsivity, attention or inhibition, and nothing clinical, and the page states this before the task begins and again in the results.
